passages.happening:
“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him. By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments” (verses 1-2).

“For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome, because everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God” (verses 3-5).
passages.hearers:
In this last chapter John ties the letter's three marks into one chain. Believing that Jesus is the Christ means being born of God. Being born of God means loving his other children. Loving God means keeping his commands. Each link holds the next. Belief, love and obedience are not three separate tests after all. They are one life.

‘His commandments are not burdensome.’ That does not mean they are easy. It means they are not a crushing weight, because God's children have a new life that wants what he wants. Jesus said, “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

Then the word ‘overcome’, nikaō, from the same root as Nikē, the Greek goddess of victory. Her images were everywhere in the cities of Asia. John says the real victory is not won by armies or by the empire. It is ‘our faith’: trust that Jesus is the Son of God. A small church in a great pagan city could hold its head up. The victory was already theirs.
passages.ot:
‘Not burdensome’ echoes Moses: “For this commandment I give you today is not too difficult for you or beyond your reach” (Deuteronomy 30:11).

And the psalms delight in God's law rather than resenting it: “I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8).
passages.asks: Ask whether you experience God's commands as a weight or as a way to live. Ask how your faith, your love and your obedience belong together. And ask what in the world around you feels too strong to overcome, and what John says about it.

passages.t: The Spirit, the water and the blood
passages.happening:
“This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ—not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement” (verses 6-8).

“Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony that God has given about His Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him; whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given about His Son. And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life” (verses 9-12).
passages.hearers:
‘By water and blood.’ This is one of the harder phrases in the letter. Many readers think it is best understood against the teachers who had left. If they held, as Irenaeus says Cerinthus did, that the divine Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism but left before his death, they would say that Christ came ‘by water’, the baptism, but not ‘by blood’, the cross. John insists: not by water alone, but by water and blood. The same Son of God who was baptised also died. Other readers connect the water and blood with the flow of blood and water from Jesus' side at the cross (John 19:34), or with baptism and the Lord's Supper.

Then John speaks of testimony, or witness. The word is marturia, evidence given in a court to establish what is true. Israel's law required two or three witnesses. John names three that agree: the Spirit, the water and the blood. If courts accept human witnesses, how much more should God's witness about his Son be believed.

And the witness comes down to one sentence. ‘God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.’ Life is not a reward handed out for good behaviour. It is found in a person. Whoever has him has life.
passages.ot:
John draws on the law's rule about witnesses: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15).

And the life found in God is the psalm's: “For with You is the fountain of life” (Psalm 36:9). Moses set the choice before Israel in the same terms: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19).
passages.hard:
Older Bibles have more words at verses 7 and 8. Why are they not here?

The King James Version reads, ‘For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one.’ The BSB, like most modern translations, reads simply, ‘For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood’.

The words about the three in heaven came into the text through Latin copies. They first appear in Latin writings of the late 300s, and they appear in only a handful of late Greek manuscripts, some of them in the margin. Erasmus left them out of his printed Greek New Testament in 1516 and put them into his third edition in 1522, and from there they passed into the King James. The Greek theologians of the fourth-century debates about the Trinity never quoted them, because their Bibles did not have them. Most modern translations have taken them out, including those made by scholars who confess the Trinity.

Some Christians who hold to the Textus Receptus, the printed Greek text behind the King James, still receive the longer words, resting their case on the Latin tradition and on God's providence over the text the church used. Most others judge that the words were not part of what John wrote.

Either way, the doctrine of the Trinity never rested on this verse. It was confessed at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 without it, and it is taught in passages whose text is not in doubt, such as Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14. The guide How We Got the New Testament says more.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the Son of God truly died, and did not only seem to. Ask whose witness about Jesus you have believed. And ask whether you have the Son, and so have life.

passages.happening:
“I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (verse 13).

“And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Here is the letter's purpose sentence. John's Gospel was written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31). This letter is written to people who already believe, ‘so that you may know that you have eternal life’.

That is why the whole letter was written. The tests of belief, obedience and love were not meant to leave readers anxious. They were meant to show people who had been shaken that the faith they had was the real thing. Those who left had claimed a deeper knowledge. John says: you are the ones who know.

The confidence spills over into prayer. ‘If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us.’ This is not a promise that every wish will be granted. ‘According to His will’ is the key. Children who know their father's heart ask for what he wants to give, and they can be sure he hears.
passages.ot:
The psalms are full of confidence that God hears: “The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry” (Psalm 34:15).

And the hope of eternal life with God shines in them too: “You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand” (Psalm 16:11).
passages.hard:
Can a Christian really know that he has eternal life? And what about prayers that seem unanswered?

John says yes to the first. He writes ‘so that you may know’. Christians explain assurance differently. Reformed teaching holds that true believers will persevere and may grow in assurance through God's promises, the Spirit's witness and the fruit of grace, though it may be clouded for a time. Wesleyans stress the Spirit's direct witness that believers are God's children. Lutherans point the troubled to Christ in the preached word and the sacraments. Catholic teaching speaks of firm hope and confidence in God's mercy, while holding that no one can know with complete certainty, without a special revelation, that he will persevere to the end. These notes do not choose. All of them read John as writing to give confidence, not fear, and all of them ground it in Christ, not in the strength of our feelings.

On prayer, ‘according to His will’ matters. Jesus himself prayed, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39). A prayer that is not answered as we hoped does not mean God did not hear, or that we lacked faith.

If you have prayed for someone to be rescued, from illness, from danger, from prison, from death, and the rescue did not come, this chapter does not say your prayer was too weak. The three friends in Daniel said God was able to deliver them, “But even if He does not” (Daniel 3:18), they would still trust him. Grief and confusion at such a loss are not a lack of faith. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you know that you have eternal life, and what your confidence rests on. Ask whether you pray as a child who trusts his father's will. And ask whom you could help to know what John wanted his readers to know.

passages.t: The sin that leads to death
passages.happening: “If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin. All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
John has just spoken of confidence in prayer. Now he gives an example: praying for a brother or sister who is caught in sin. His instruction is simple. If you see it, pray, and God will give life.

Then he adds a puzzling line about ‘a sin that leads to death’, and says he is not telling his readers to pray about that. He does not explain what he means. His readers may have known. We do not, and it is wise to say so.

Notice what John stresses. All wrongdoing is sin; he does not make light of it. But not every sin leads to death. Most of what believers see in one another is the kind of sin for which they should pray, and God will give life.
passages.ot:
The law drew a line between sins done in weakness or without knowing, and sins done in open defiance. For unintentional sin there was atonement (Numbers 15:27-28). But “the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD” (Numbers 15:30).

And the psalm prays for help against both: “Who can discern his own errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults. Keep Your servant also from willful sins” (Psalm 19:12-13).
passages.hard:
What is ‘the sin that leads to death’? Could I have committed it?

John does not define it, and Christians have read it in several ways. These notes do not choose. Some take it as sin that God judges with bodily death, as with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) or the Corinthians who were sick (1 Corinthians 11:30). Others take it as a deliberate and final rejection of Christ, like that shown by the teachers who left the churches and denied the Son. Some connect it with Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28-29). The law's line between unintentional sins and sins done ‘defiantly’ may lie in the background. Many readers think the letter's own setting points to the second reading, since its whole concern is with those who denied that Jesus is the Christ.

Some things should be said plainly. John does not forbid anyone to pray for anyone. He simply does not command it in this case, and his weight falls the other way: pray for the brother or sister who is sinning. Nothing in these verses lets a reader decide that a particular person has committed this sin, or say what any person's state before God is. That belongs to God alone. And nothing here makes anyone's illness or death a sign of God's judgment. When his disciples asked whose sin had caused a man's blindness, Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3).

Many Christians have been afraid that they committed an unforgivable sin. A long pastoral tradition answers that the fear itself is a sign that the heart has not turned hard in this way.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you have seen struggling with sin, and whether you have prayed for them or only judged them. Ask whether you are carrying a fear about your own sin that you need to bring to God and to someone you trust. And ask what it would mean to believe that God gives life.

passages.t: What we know, and the last warning
passages.happening:
“We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him. We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one” (verses 18-19).

“And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends with three sentences that each begin ‘We know’. They gather up what the readers can be sure of.

First, God's children do not settle into sin, and they are kept. ‘The One who was born of God’ is most likely Christ himself, who guards them so that the evil one cannot touch them.

Second, we belong to God, even though the world as a system lies under the evil one's power.

Third, the Son of God has come and given understanding, so that we may know the true God. And then a remarkable line: ‘He is the true God and eternal life.’ Grammarians debate whether ‘He’ means the Son or the Father. Many readers, noting that the nearest name is Jesus Christ, and that the letter began by calling him ‘the eternal life’ (1:2), take it as one of the clearest confessions in the New Testament that Jesus is God.

The last line is sudden: ‘Little children, keep yourselves from idols.’ There is no goodbye. In Ephesus, the temple of Artemis was one of the wonders of the world, and images of gods and emperors filled streets and homes and marketplaces. Trade guilds held meals in honour of their gods. John's warning may also reach wider, to any false picture of God, including the false Christ of those who had left. After showing who the true God is, John warns against every substitute.
passages.ot:
The warning against idols is the first commandment in another voice: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3). The prophets mocked idols that cannot see or save: “All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless” (Isaiah 44:9).

And the true God is the living God: “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King” (Jeremiah 10:10).
passages.hard:
‘He is the true God and eternal life.’ Does this verse call Jesus God?

Many readers think so. The nearest name in the sentence is ‘His Son Jesus Christ’, and the letter began by calling Jesus ‘the eternal life that was with the Father’ (1:2). Others think ‘He’ refers back to the Father, ‘Him who is true’. Grammarians on both sides are careful scholars.

Either way, the faith of the church does not rest on one verse. The New Testament calls Jesus God in other places, such as John 1:1 and John 20:28, and the church confesses it in the Nicene Creed: Jesus Christ is ‘very God of very God’, who ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. 1 John is one of the places that confession comes from, and its insistence on a Christ who truly came in the flesh is why the church would not let go of either half.
passages.asks: Ask which of the three ‘we know’ sentences you most need to hold onto. Ask what idol, visible or not, is most likely to take the place of the true God in your life. And ask what it means for you that the Son of God has come so that you may know him.
